vignette:
He is a 71-year-old Oceania man who comes to therapy with the kind of careful composure that has helped him get through most of his life. He is married, works part-time as a cashier, and has spent decades being the person who keeps things moving, who smiles, who does not make trouble. In sessions, he speaks slowly and often with long pauses, as if he is weighing each word against memories that still feel close.

The traumatic event he describes happened while he was still working full-time. He was driving home after a late shift when he came upon a serious road accident. One car had crossed the center line, and there were people trapped inside. He remembers the smell first, then the sound of a woman calling for her child. He stops there when he tells it, looking down at his hands. He says he got out to help before emergency services arrived because “there was no one else there.” He remembers trying to calm a boy who was crying and asking if his mother was awake. The image that stays with him most is the child’s small hand on the window, leaving a print on the glass. He says that even now he can see it clearly, as if the scene is frozen in front of him.

In the days after, he returns to work and tells almost no one what he saw. He thinks he should be able to handle it. He has always been practical, a man who worked long hours, raised a family, and kept his feelings private. But as he goes back to the checkout counter, he notices that ordinary sounds make him jump. The squeal of shopping trolleys, a slammed car door in the parking lot, the sudden cry of a child in the aisle all send a jolt through his body. He keeps scanning the store for danger without meaning to. He begins to feel uneasy around intersections and avoids driving that route home. If he does pass that road, he grips the steering wheel until his knuckles ache and tells himself to breathe.

At night, the accident returns to him in fragments. He wakes with his heart racing, sometimes sweating so heavily that his shirt sticks to his back. There are nights when he sees the scene the moment he closes his eyes, and he lies awake listening to his wife sleep beside him. He does not want to disturb her, so he turns quietly and stares into the dark. He starts sitting up later and later, watching television without really taking it in, because if he goes to bed too early the images come faster. He becomes tired at work, but when he has a customer in front of him he forces himself to be polite and steady. He says people probably think he is simply getting older and slower.

Over time, he becomes more distant from the parts of life that used to feel easy. He does not like family gatherings as much because there are children there, and their voices remind him of the boy in the car. He notices himself leaving the room when someone begins talking about accidents, injuries, or funerals. His wife tells him he seems “far away,” and she is right; he often feels as though part of him is still standing at the roadside, trying to help while another part is trapped in the present. He feels irritated more easily now, especially when he is tired, and afterward he feels ashamed of his sharpness. He misses the version of himself who could laugh more easily and sleep through the night.

Even now, years later, the memory has not faded in the way he expected. It is not a story from the past so much as an experience that keeps intruding into ordinary moments. A siren passing outside the shop, the smell of hot metal on a summer day, a child crying in the supermarket aisle can bring the whole scene rushing back. He knows this is why he has started to feel smaller in the world, less certain of where he is and what might happen next. Still, he keeps showing up to work, greeting customers, counting change, and moving through the day with the same steady hands he used at the roadside, as if routine itself might hold the memories at bay for a little while.
